strengths: The paper offers a clean, well-motivated conceptual framework: it defines a formal notion of 'world model' via consistency/sensitivity properties over prompt-intent pairs, then relaxes this into a practical 'sufficient world model' definition using an evaluator function, which is a sensible way to make an abstract philosophical question operational.

The variance decomposition (PS/AS/MU, summing to one) is intuitive, interpretable, and provides a principled way to disentangle sources of response variability -- a real methodological contribution beyond simple accuracy or scalar prompt-sensitivity metrics used in prior work (e.g., PSS, FormatSpread).

The empirical study is reasonably thorough: 5 domains, 15 base tasks, 5 models spanning different sizes/families, with bootstrap confidence intervals reported for every decomposition estimate, and a robustness check using an alternative (survey-style) prompt generation method in the appendix.

The paper situates itself carefully relative to closely related work (stochastic parrots critique, prompt robustness/spurious-features literature, and especially Vafa et al.'s DFA-based world-model test), clarifying what is genuinely new about the distribution-aware, evaluator-tunable approach.
The appendix extension to discrete/categorical outputs via an information-theoretic (entropy/mutual-information) analogue is a nice generalization that broadens applicability beyond numeric tasks.

Honest reporting of mixed/modest findings (larger models not uniformly better, domain-dependent robustness) rather than overselling the result, and discussion of practical implications (fairness auditing via Articulation Sensitivity) is a plus.
weaknesses: Nearly the entire evaluation pipeline (translation-based paraphrasing, intent-preservation verification, and numeric answer extraction) is delegated to GPT-4o-mini with no human validation or inter-rater checks; errors or biases introduced at any of these stages could confound the PS/AS/MU estimates, and this is not empirically assessed.

The operationalization of 'intent change' in most tasks is simply varying a single numeric slot in an otherwise fixed template (e.g., income level, number of boxes, mg of medication). This is a narrow and somewhat mechanical notion of 'purpose,' arguably closer to testing numeric input-sensitivity/interpolation than to testing a rich notion of user intent as motivated in the conceptual sections.

Reducing free-form model responses to a single extracted scalar discards most of the information in the response and privileges tasks with a well-defined 'bottom-line number,' which narrows the class of tasks to which the method can be applied and may bias which failures/successes are visible.

The central empirical claims (larger models generally have higher PS) are weak and inconsistent across domains and models (e.g., 70B is not uniformly best, Gemma 27B sometimes underperforms Gemma 12B), and the paper does not provide a formal cross-model/cross-domain statistical test of these comparisons, relying instead on visual inspection of bar charts.

In most reported tables, Model Uncertainty (MU) dominates the decomposition (often >0.7-0.9), meaning PS and AS -- the terms motivating the entire framework -- are frequently small, limiting the discriminative power and practical significance of the diagnostic in the tested settings.

Only a handful of models (five) and a single model per size tier are tested, and the alternative survey-based paraphrase generation is only validated for two models/four domains in the appendix, leaving open whether the qualitative conclusions are robust to the specific choice of models or paraphrase-generation method.

The heavy formal notation in Section 2/3 (world model definitions, sufficient world model, R^2-based decomposition) is essentially reformulating a one-way ANOVA/variance-components model; while pedagogically useful, the level of formalism may overstate the technical novelty relative to the (conceptually simple) underlying statistical method.

strengths: Clean, interpretable theoretical framework: the PS + AS + MU = 1 variance decomposition is mathematically well-motivated (via standard R^2 decomposition) and yields an intuitive 'signal-to-noise' (MVS) summary statistic that is easy to communicate to practitioners.

The paper carefully develops two nested definitions (a strict 'world model' and a more usable 'sufficient world model' relative to an evaluator), and situates this work thoughtfully against related literatures (stochastic parrots critique, RL world models, DFA/Myhill-Nerode based evaluation of Vafa et al., prompt-sensitivity/format-robustness literature), showing good scholarly awareness of adjacent work.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: 5 domains x 3 tasks x 5 models x 3 intent values x 50 paraphrases x 50 samples, with bootstrap confidence intervals reported per task/model in the appendix, and a secondary survey-style paraphrase generation method used as a robustness check that yields qualitatively similar patterns.

Honest and nuanced reporting of findings: rather than overselling a clean 'bigger is better' story, the paper reports that improvements from scale are inconsistent across domains and often modest, and explicitly flags this as a limitation rather than smoothing it over.

Extension to discrete/categorical outputs via an information-theoretic (entropy/mutual-information) analogue of the decomposition broadens applicability beyond purely numeric responses and shows the framework's generality.
Practical framing connecting AS to fairness/dialect robustness concerns is a plausible and valuable applied motivation for the metric.
weaknesses: Substantial gap between the rich, abstract notion of 'intent' motivated in Section 2 (e.g., the coin-flip/positive-negative equivalence example) and its actual operationalization in experiments, which reduces to varying a single numeric slot in an otherwise fixed template (income level, box count, medication quantity). This is closer to testing sensitivity to an explicit input variable than to testing whether the model infers a latent, unstated communicative goal, which is a weaker and less novel claim than the framing suggests.

The Model Uncertainty (MU) term dominates in nearly all reported results (often 0.6-0.95 of total variance, per Tables 1-5), meaning the headline PS/AS comparison is being made over a small residual share of the total variance; the paper does not discuss how this affects the reliability or interpretability of cross-model PS/AS comparisons, nor does it test whether observed PS/AS differences across models are statistically distinguishable once MU's dominance is accounted for.

Only 15 base tasks total (3 per domain) with only 3 discrete intent values each; this is a small and somewhat ad hoc task set from which broad claims about 'world models' across five real-world domains are drawn, limiting generalizability and statistical power, especially given the observed inconsistency across tasks/domains/models.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o-mini for three separate roles (paraphrase generation via translation, intent-equivalence verification, and numeric answer extraction) introduces compounding, uncharacterized noise and potential systematic bias into the pipeline; no human validation of paraphrase fidelity or extraction accuracy is reported, which is a reproducibility/soundness concern given these judgments are central to defining what counts as 'same intent' and to computing the response values used in the decomposition.

The evaluator V collapses rich free-form responses to a single scalar per response (with ranges averaged and non-numeric responses discarded), discarding substantial information the model may encode in its answer; this is acknowledged as a limitation but its practical impact on the reported decomposition (e.g., bias introduced by discarding indefinite answers) is not empirically probed.

No proprietary/frontier models (e.g., GPT-4/4o, Claude, Gemini) are evaluated, only open-weight Llama and Gemma variants up to 70B, limiting how much the scaling conclusions generalize to state-of-the-art systems most relevant to 'high-stakes' deployment claims made in the introduction.

The central empirical finding is fairly modest (larger models are only somewhat, inconsistently better), which is honestly reported but also means the paper's demonstrated 'diagnostic value' is not strongly validated against any external ground truth of model quality or downstream task performance—there is no correlation analysis linking PS/AS/MVS to independently-verified measures of model competence or reliability.
